extracted.intended_audience: Reuters journalists, sports reporters and sub-editors (sports desks and bureaux)
extracted.subtask_description: Editorial and legal guidance for producing Reuters sports copy: what to cover, how to structure match and event stories, style/wording rules, and when to escalate legally risky items to editors. Covers soccer, tennis, winter sports and specialised attention-editor rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of confederation acronyms
rubrics_metrics.description: Reuters uses confederation acronyms with a brief explanation (e.g. European soccer's ruling body UEFA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use acronyms such as UEFA, AFC, CAF, CONCACAF, CONMEBOL and OFC with a brief explanatory phrase on first reference. Note the hierarchical relationship under FIFA and that tensions between bodies can provide copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soccer coverage depth by country
rubrics_metrics.description: Depth of regular Reuters coverage of domestic leagues in Europe depends on the soccer profile of the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover England, France, Italy, Spain and Germany in great depth with previews, injury news before each weekend/midweek, fast leads, brief match reports, updates and extra updates/quotes pieces plus sidebars as merited. Cup games: highlight big matches in early rounds; more coverage for FA Cup in England. Staff some cup semis/finals and discuss arrangements with soccer editor/desk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage of other European leagues
rubrics_metrics.description: Other important European leagues get weekly league reports and fixtures/results; lesser leagues file only for significant developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File east European round-ups on Monday covering named countries. Stories involving leagues not in the top five should be slugged BC-SOCCER-EUROPE/<country>. Bureaux should contribute two or three-paragraph briefs for London round-ups (injury, transfer, human interest, quotes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin American soccer coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate stories on Argentine, Brazilian and Mexican leagues and a round-up of the others, coordinated in Rio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Round-ups usually run early Monday. Accept on- and off-field stories from any centres and from the Spanish Language Service. Be careful with Latin American player names (see Players' names guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: African & Asian soccer coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Africa and Asia have coordinated coverage with weekly round-ups and selected previews/wraps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: African coverage coordinated by Johannesburg; South African league results run. Asian coverage includes Japan's J-league and South Korea's K-league with weekly wraps; other countries covered on merit as interest grows (China etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Champions League matchday format
rubrics_metrics.description: On matchday: a four-paragraph story on the whistle, followed by a 350-400 word update with match detail then a quotes piece after managers' news conference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Desk issues a preview package early the day before matches. Bureaux should advise Sports Desk who is staffing/backstopping. File breaking news (injuries, fresh quotes) as they happen; London will update the package. Managers/coaches are required to give news conferences and supply players for mixed zone. For semi-finals/finals and high-profile games coverage is boosted and Sports Desk will advise. Trunk can be updated with extra background/stats or telling quote on merit; follow-up story early next day to throw the story forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: UEFA Cup and similar competitions coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Variable quality in early rounds; Sports Desk provides preview and will advise bureaux on input required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File spot stories with team news, big name injuries. Storify newsworthy items such as mass sendings off, big scores, hat-tricks. London will run a wrap and advise requirements; later rounds need match reports, monitored off television or staffed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Libertadores and other continental cups
rubrics_metrics.description: Run in similar way to Champions League but qualifying varies by country; coordinated wrap coverage by regional desks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SLS covers all matches from the first round group stage with a lead; Rio files a single wrap on the night's play. Knockout stages similar to Champions League coverage. African Champions Cup and Confederations Cup coverage coordinated with previews and wraps.

rubrics_metrics.name: International tournament staffing
rubrics_metrics.description: World Cup finals and continental cup finals are special projects with their own teams of reporters on the ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualifying competitions last up to three years and require detailed coverage from participating datelines. Draws for qualifying staffed from London or by regional specialists. Follow desk guidance on which matches require full staffing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Squad announcement format
rubrics_metrics.description: Before matches file stories on squad announcements, listing full squad with first names and surnames and club in brackets, under goalkeepers, defenders, midfielders and forwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct Reuters style for clubs (do NOT add the country name to the club, e.g. Thierry Henry (Barcelona) NOT Thierry Henry (Barcelona, Spain)). For main matches follow with a story detailing who has been left out/included since last match, injuries, suspensions. The story should contain the word 'squad' in the headline and should add the squad at the bottom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matchday reporting for internationals
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should contact the desk as soon as they are at the venue/in position and file a four-paragraph lead on the whistle for important matches with updates thereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File bare bones with ramifications for qualifying, then an update usually ~350 words with match description as soon as possible. On high-profile matches may squirt quick relevant quotes/statistics into a second update; high-profile games may need only six paras total. Quotes piece after managers' news conference/mixed zone; follow-up next day as needed. Consult London desk on complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendlies coverage guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendlies are matches not part of an official competition but can be intense; coverage level depends on teams involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat friendlies between leading nations, big rivals, or tournament participants almost the same as competitive internationals (squad announcement, previews, lineups, fast lead, update). For friendlies between lesser powers consult the desk on level of cover required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfers reporting principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Reuters does not indulge in idle speculation about transfers; reporters must develop a sense of likelihood and avoid rumor-mongering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is no usable source speak to the Sports Desk first. Newspaper pickups may be only source but use judgment; keep records of most expensive signings. If in doubt consult Sports Desk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimonials/benefits/club friendlies policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Not generally covered except when they have specific news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate on merit (e.g. top name retirement). If in doubt, consult the desk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age-group tournaments coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Cover World Youth Cup (under-20) finals as an assignment, limited coverage of under-17 World Cup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File match reports for those assigned events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Olympic soccer coverage policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not routinely cover Olympic qualifying competitions but file merited stories arising from Olympic qualifying; cover Olympic finals from the host city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occasional merited stories acceptable; report both men's and women's Olympic tournaments when assigned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women's soccer coverage level
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally not covered routinely; maintain low-level coverage of women's World Cup; offbeat brights, features and strong news angles welcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the women's game lacks sponsorship/investment, only strong newsworthy items or features should be filed. Use judgment on merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penpix length
rubrics_metrics.description: Penpix (player profiles) should be brief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three or four lines on each player before World Cup and continental championship finals as well as major Cup finals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factboxes usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Issue factboxes regularly for soccer on leading players/coaches, clubs in trouble, disasters, accidents, deaths and winners' stats for tournaments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before/after big tournaments or cup finals run stats with previous winners etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soccer style points (wording & usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific word/phrase capitalization and compound-word rules for soccer terminology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: 'free kick' two words; 'team mate' two words; 'goal kick' two words; 'extra time' two words; 'spot kick' two words; 'left back' two words; 'centre forward' two words; 'right wing' two words; 'wing back' two words; 'Goalkeeper' one word (also 'keeper' with no apostrophe); 'Halftime' one word; 'kickoff' one word; 'playoff' one word; 'Champions League' upper case, no apostrophe; 'Nations Cup' upper case, no apostrophe; 'Premier League' upper case; 'Primera Liga' capitals; 'Ligue 1' capitals; 'Serie A' capitals; 'Bundesliga' Germany; 'keeper' no apostrophe; 'Group Three' caps for qualifying groups; use 'Defeat by/loss to' not 'defeat to'; use 'metres' not yards/feet; avoid clichés like 'hard fought' and 'crucial'; ban 'star, icon, legend' and 'veteran'—give age or years; use 'v' not 'vs' or 'versus'; 'stadiums' not 'stadia'; 'FA' takes singular verb; 'FIFA' takes singular verb; 'UEFA' takes singular verb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Players' names conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on how to refer to players from different cultures (Brazilian, Spanish, Portuguese, Latin American, Dutch, Turkish, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadly: Brazilian, Spanish and some Portuguese players often referred to by a single name or nickname (e.g. Pele, Ronaldo, Ronaldinho). Composite names (e.g. Roberto Carlos) or both names (Paulo Ferreira) should be used throughout. In Spanish-speaking countries use the penultimate name as the surname; in Portuguese-speaking countries the last name. Some Latam players may use both surnames (e.g. Guillermo Barros Schelotto) or nicknames; Dutch players like Jimmy Floyd Hasselbaink are always known in full; Turkish players often known by first name at second reference. If in doubt consult the desk or bureau of origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tennis coverage priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage varies by tournament type and player involvement; desk will advise on requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For tournaments outside the Masters with a top-five player present usually ask for an early lead and a wrap at end of day; big developments (top seed knocked out, top-level injury) can merit quick 4-paragraph separates. Offbeat sidebars and interviews welcome. Bigger tournaments (Masters, grand slams) require beefed-up coverage with stats boxes and more frequent leads/newsbreaks. Doubles generally not covered unless newsworthy; Davis Cup world group matches need stories after each match and a wrap with quotes. Home-country angles (interviews, human interest, injuries, personal stories) are useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tennis style points and score formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Wording/capitalization and score formatting rules for tennis copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'tiebreak, backhand, forehand, topspin, wildcard, netcord' are one word; 'double fault, drop shot, match point, set point, break point, prize money' are two words. 'Claycourt, grasscourt, hardcourt' one word as adjectives, two words when adjective + noun. 'grand slam' lower case; 'Masters Series' capitals. Avoid clichés ('crashed out', 'marathon match', 'hard fought', 'dug deep', 'bounced back'). Show sets without commas (e.g. 3-6 6-4 6-4) and give winner's details first even if focus is on the loser. Try to get scores into the first paragraph and give the score rather than just 'beat' or 'won in straight sets'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Winter sports coverage principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Winter sports are covered primarily at major events; many are covered only on merit outside Olympics/World Champs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alpine skiing is covered in depth with women's races given equal importance. Minor winter sports (luge, bobsleigh, ski jumping, freestyle, speed skating, biathlon) covered mostly for Olympics or serious incidents/scandals. Report figure skating at World, European and Four Continents championships; ice hockey covered at world championship pool A level. Look for colour stories, rivalries, injuries and scandals (doping, scoring controversies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alpine skiing reporting specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Include weather, course information and types of snow; report training runs and timings; file urgent winner reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include basic course info (name, length, number of gates). Cover training runs (two training days), publish final training timings and note starting order advantage. For Downhill and Super-G file four-paragraph story after winner bulletin, then updates, factbox on winner and any sidebars. Previews and aftermath stories as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slalom/giant slalom reporting rules
rubrics_metrics.description: In two-legged events file timing and brief descriptive after first leg and urgent winner/places after second leg.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not say someone 'won' the first leg — say they were 'leading'. File timings and brief describe after first leg; the top 30 go in reverse order for second leg. Urgent winner, second and third with four-paragraph quick lead after second leg. Results may be provisional — go with early timings, mark them provisional and update with official tag later.

rubrics_metrics.name: World Cup points allocation (Alpine skiing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Competitors earn World Cup points for placings down to 30 with a fixed points table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points: 1st 100, 2nd 80, 3rd 60, 4th 50, 5th 45, 6th 40, 7th 36, 8th 32, 9th 29, 10th 26, 11th 24, 12th 22, 13th 20, 14th 18, 15th 16, 16th 15, 17th 14, 18th 13, 19th 12, 20th 11, 21st 10, 22nd 9, 23rd 8, 24th 7, 25th 6, 26th 5, 27th 4, 28th 3, 29th 2, 30th 1. Points added at season end; discipline cups awarded to most points; overall trophy for highest total across disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Winter sports style points
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific capitalization, compound words, terminology and unit usage for winter sports copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Alpine skiing' capital A; 'super-G' lower case s, capital G; 'downhill' one word; 'schuss' defined as fast downhill run/section; 'whiteout' defined; 'to edge' as verb; 'World Cup' capitals; 'metres' always spell out (never 'm'); 'km' singular and plural not spelled out; prefer 'postpone' over 'cancel' for bad weather (most races are postponed, not cancelled); avoid using the word 'Winter' unless unavoidable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention Editor escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: Potentially risky or legally dangerous stories must be slugged ATTENTION EDITOR and sent to regional specialist editor or senior desk editor with explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Err on side of caution. Include an accompanying message explaining risks. Refer to in-house or external lawyers if required. Examples of items that may require escalation include bankruptcy stories, civil lawsuits, contentious allegations, graphic/obscene content, legally dangerous material, sensational scientific/medical breakthroughs, withdrawals and other items listed in the handbook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bankruptcy stories handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Bankruptcy stories should be slugged ATTENTION EDITOR and handled cautiously with precise terminology and company comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A company is formally bankrupt only when a court rules it so; terms (bankruptcy, insolvency, liquidation) differ by country and must be used precisely with definitions where necessary. Any potential bankruptcy report from a third party must contain comment from the company or indicate serious efforts to seek comment if unavailable. Be careful with translations (e.g. French 'faillite' vs 'banqueroute'). In the US note Chapter 11/Chapter 7 distinctions. Avoid over-colourful reporting implying hopelessness which could invite legal trouble if the company recovers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil lawsuits reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid reporting threats of lawsuits unless the parties are high profile and the case is sufficiently market-moving; slug ATTENTION EDITOR and include comment from both parties if covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the motive of the source and the risk of being used to exert pressure for settlement. If coverage is warranted slug ATTENTION EDITOR for regional editor decision. Any story about a threatened or real lawsuit must include comment from both parties; if comment isn't immediately available and there's an overriding news reason to run the story, state what efforts were made to reach the party (e.g. 'A spokesman for Company X did not respond to two voicemail messages seeking comment.').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of unnamed sources for allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not allow sources to make allegations, contentious statements or vituperative attacks behind a cloak of anonymity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If quoting unnamed sources on one side of a conflict use them only for facts, not opinions. Waive the on-the-record rule only in rare cases for senior officials making a considered policy statement who are obviously newsworthy and identifiable as officials. The story must make clear the informant volunteered the information and is an official. If a person will not speak on that basis, do not use the story.
